problem.title: Large-scale document classification
problem.context: An insurer receives between two and eight million documents a day (scanned forms, e-mails, PDFs) and classifies each one into one of 60 claim types with an LLM-based classifier. Volume varies strongly over the year: storm season brings four times the usual load. Three teams use the results: claims handling, fraud investigation and analytics. The documents contain personal data.

requirements.text: Classify every incoming document into a claim type, with a confidence.
Deliver the results to the three consuming teams.
Send the documents the classifier is unsure about to human review, and use the reviewers' corrections to improve the classifier.
During storm season, at eight million documents a day, every document is classified within two hours of arrival.
When classification quality drops for one claim type (for example, after a form changes its layout), operators see it within one day.
The classification costs less than 0.2 cents per document on average over the year.
A consuming team can change how it processes the results without the other teams or the classifier having to change.
The documents contain personal data and may not leave the EU.
The classifier uses an LLM from the insurer's approved provider, in its EU region.

approaches.idea: What if scheduled bulk inference is the primary scaling and cost-control mechanism?
What if a cheap-first cascade preserves approved-LLM accuracy while reducing average inference cost?
What if per-document autoscaling provides the simplest path to the two-hour peak target?
approaches.dropped_because: One paid LLM invocation per document gives weaker average-cost control than selective inference, and per-document calls add concurrency and delivery pressure.

approaches.idea: What if a regional queue with microbatch workers combines burst absorption with bounded provider concurrency?

values: Inference architecture: Scheduled bulk inference
Uncertainty and learning: Confidence threshold with daily reviewer feedback
Results integration: Durable result event stream
Quality monitoring: Daily type-level quality dashboard
trajectory.hypothesis: Bulk windows should improve provider utilization and control average cost (Q1,Q3); event publication should isolate consumers (Q4).
trajectory.observation: Batching helps utilization, but peak scheduling and ordinary daily dashboards do not establish the two-hour or one-day targets; feedback is not prioritized.

values: Inference architecture: Cheap-first cascade with approved LLM fallback
Uncertainty and learning: Confidence threshold with daily reviewer feedback
Results integration: Durable result event stream
Quality monitoring: Daily type-level quality dashboard
trajectory.hypothesis: Routing easy cases away from the LLM should reduce average cost while preserving classification coverage (R1,Q3); targeted review and alerts should improve R3 and Q2.
trajectory.observation: Selective inference offers a credible cost path, but daily review and aggregate monitoring leave feedback prioritization and type-level detection weaker; peak throughput and provider pricing still need measurement.

values: Inference architecture: Per-document autoscaled approved-LLM workers
Uncertainty and learning: Confidence threshold with daily reviewer feedback
Results integration: Direct team-specific APIs
Quality monitoring: Daily type-level quality dashboard
trajectory.hypothesis: Autoscaling should handle variable volume and direct APIs should deliver results quickly (Q1,R2).
trajectory.observation: One provider call per document has no credible path to the strict average-cost ceiling, and team-specific APIs couple producers to consumers. Refining worker scaling cannot fix those structural problems.

values: Inference architecture: Scheduled bulk inference
Uncertainty and learning: Confidence threshold with active-learning review queue
Results integration: Durable result event stream
Quality monitoring: Per-type drift and labeled-outcome alerts
trajectory.hypothesis: Keep bulk utilization but prioritize uncertain reviews and add type-level signals to close the main R3 and Q2 gaps.
trajectory.observation: Feedback and monitoring now address their requirements, while batch-window latency remains the main uncertainty for Q1.

values: Inference architecture: Cheap-first cascade with approved LLM fallback
Uncertainty and learning: Confidence threshold with active-learning review queue

trajectory.hypothesis: Calibrating the cascade against type-specific review outcomes should protect R1 and Q2 while retaining the expected Q3 advantage.
trajectory.observation: This remains the strongest cost-oriented combination, though empirical calibration is needed to show both quality and cost targets.

values: Inference architecture: Per-document autoscaled approved-LLM workers

Results integration: Durable result event stream

trajectory.hypothesis: Decoupled events and better review signals should fix Q4 and Q2 without changing the per-document inference model.
trajectory.observation: The refinements improve integration and feedback but do not change the structural cost exposure; the approach is dropped.

values: Inference architecture: Regional queue with microbatch approved-LLM workers

trajectory.hypothesis: A regional queue can absorb bursts and microbatches can bound provider concurrency while active review and alerts meet R3 and Q2.
trajectory.observation: Queueing offers a plausible operating envelope across demand spikes; microbatch sizing and provider limits must be validated against the latency target.

values: Inference architecture: Scheduled bulk inference with priority lanes
Uncertainty and learning: Confidence threshold with active-learning review queue
Results integration: Durable result event stream
Quality monitoring: Per-type drift and labeled-outcome alerts
trajectory.hypothesis: Peak-capacity reservations and prioritized review improve Q1 while retaining the strengths of bulk processing.
trajectory.observation: Reservations reduce scheduling risk but do not remove the dependence on batch-window duration; no new requirement is improved decisively.

values: Inference architecture: Selective cascade with reserved LLM fallback

Quality monitoring: Per-type drift and labeled-outcome alerts
trajectory.hypothesis: Per-type thresholds should reduce unnecessary LLM fallbacks while maintaining quality and catching type-specific degradation.
trajectory.observation: Threshold calibration strengthens the cost rationale, with cost and recall still requiring measured validation on representative documents.

values: Inference architecture: Regional queue with adaptive microbatch workers
Uncertainty and learning: Confidence threshold with active-learning review queue
Results integration: Durable result event stream
Quality monitoring: Per-type drift and labeled-outcome alerts
trajectory.hypothesis: Reserved storm capacity and idempotent publication should improve Q1 and reliable R2 delivery.
trajectory.observation: Queue controls and replay-safe publication make the design operationally resilient, but provider service limits and end-to-end latency remain to be benchmarked.

alternatives.name: Reserved bulk classification
alternatives.summary: Schedule approved-provider EU inference in bulk windows, reserve peak capacity, publish durable result events, and route uncertain cases to prioritized review with per-type alerts.

choices.reason: Priority lanes and peak reservations protect urgent storm-season work while preserving bulk utilization in the approved EU region.

adrs.title: How should inference absorb demand while controlling LLM spend?
adrs.context: The system must classify millions of documents, meet a two-hour storm-season deadline and stay under a strict annual average cost. All paths must keep personal data in the EU and use the insurer's approved provider in its EU region. Actual throughput and pricing require workload benchmarks.

options.name: Reserved bulk inference
values: Inference architecture: Scheduled bulk inference with priority lanes
pros: Batching can improve utilization and cost predictability.
Peak reservations make capacity planning explicit.
cons: Long batch windows can consume the two-hour latency budget.
options.reason: Choose when predictable bulk utilization outweighs tighter response-time needs.

options.name: Selective LLM cascade
values: Inference architecture: Selective cascade with reserved LLM fallback
pros: Clear cases can avoid LLM expense.
Approved LLM remains available for ambiguous documents.
cons: The inexpensive stage needs validated accuracy and calibrated routing.
options.reason: Choose when reducing paid LLM volume is the leading cost strategy.

options.name: Queued microbatch inference
values: Inference architecture: Regional queue with adaptive microbatch workers
pros: Queues absorb bursts and regulate provider concurrency.
Reserved capacity can protect peak throughput.
cons: Queue delay and microbatch sizing must be measured against the deadline.
options.reason: Choose when buffering and bounded concurrency are central operating needs.

adrs.title: How should uncertain classifications feed human review and model improvement?
adrs.context: Every document needs a classification and confidence, while low-confidence cases need timely human correction. Corrections should create useful learning data without overwhelming reviewers.

options.name: Daily threshold review
values: Uncertainty and learning: Confidence threshold with daily reviewer feedback
cons: Daily routing can delay correction and does not prioritize informative examples.
options.reason: Superseded by active-learning prioritization for more timely and useful feedback.

options.name: Prioritized active-learning queue
values: Uncertainty and learning: Confidence threshold with active-learning review queue
pros: Prioritization directs reviewer effort toward informative cases.
cons: Needs threshold calibration and a review workflow sized to incoming uncertainty.
options.reason: Use corrected labels to improve the classifier while managing review demand.

adrs.title: How should results reach teams and quality issues become visible?
adrs.context: Three teams consume classification results and need to evolve independently. Operators need to notice claim-type-specific quality drops within one day, including changes caused by forms or layouts.

options.name: Team-specific APIs with daily aggregate dashboard
values: Results integration: Direct team-specific APIs
Quality monitoring: Daily type-level quality dashboard
pros: Direct calls can be straightforward for a small integration.
cons: Team-specific interfaces couple consumers to the classifier.
Daily aggregate views can miss timely type-level signals.
options.reason: Does not support loose coupling and timely per-type alerting as well as event delivery and labeled outcomes.

options.name: Durable events with per-type outcome alerts
values: Results integration: Durable result event stream
Quality monitoring: Per-type drift and labeled-outcome alerts
pros: Consumers evolve independently against stable events.
Drift and reviewed labels can expose type-specific degradation.
cons: Requires event schema governance and representative outcome labels.
options.reason: Use durable delivery and type-level monitoring to meet independent consumption and timely diagnosis.
